newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Deal talk aids Lyonnaise,Suez down.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deal talk aids Lyonnaise,Suez down.

text.p: Shares in holding company Cie de Suez see-sawed on Monday as the stock market bet that a rumoured merger with water utility Lyonnaise des Eaux was on the cards and focused on how the deal would be carried out.
Suez sank 1.11 percent to close at 277.3 francs after earlier rising to a high of 291.0 as the market bet Suez would be the one to make an offer.

Lyonnaise shares closed at 574 francs, up 2.32 percent, in busy trading fuelled by a weekend report in Saturday's Le Monde newspaper that the two firms hoped to present a merger plan to an April 1 meeting of the Suez board.
Both companies refused to comment on the report, which said Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod and Suez chairman Gerard Mestrallet were spending the weekend working on a merger deal.

Glassmaker Saint Gobain, which holds a little over six percent of Suez's capital and whose chairman Jean-Louis Beffa was said by Le Monde to be involved in the talks, also had no comment on a possible merger, a spokeswoman said.
But traders sounded confident a deal was in the works which would create France's ninth biggest company with a market capitalisation of around 79 billion francs ($13.9 billion).
"The market is no longer wondering whether it will happen but when and at what terms," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Jean-Baptiste Bellon.

"The market is betting on the fact that the merger will take place and that Suez will absorb Lyonnaise des Eaux, which means Suez will have to pay a premium to encourage that merger," said a trader. "I couldn't understand why Suez was up this morning."

Analysts said any merger was likely to be structured to enable Suez to bid for Lyonnaise as it is the larger firm and has cash and important unused tax losses which would be lost if Suez were acquired by Lyonnaise.

"We are expecting Suez to offer a share swap for Lyonnaise due to Suez's three billion francs in unused tax losses," said Dupont-Denant analyst John Honore. Suez already owns 16.8 percent of Lyonnaise.

Market rumours that a deal was being worked out gained credibility last week when Etienne Davignon, chairman of Suez unit Societe Generale de Belgique SA, acknowledged a merger was possible though he said no decision had been made.
Analysts said the deal would help give direction to Suez, which has lost its raison d'etre after selling most of its assets, including its crown jewel, Banque Indosuez.
The big attraction for Lyonnaise would be Suez's cash hoard and its handful of industrial holdings.
Lyonnaise, whose main businesses are water contracts, construction and energy, has high hopes for global expansion but lacks the resources to finance growth, analysts said.
The possibility of a merger has worried Lyonnaise's rival Generale des Eaux, which fears the combination would produce not a bigger competitor but a financially stronger one.
Generale des Eaux has said a merger would harm Suez's minority shareholders but denied a report it was considering a hostile bid for Suez to block any pact.

Talk of a merger has also worried Belgian officials who fear that a deal would give France control of Tractebel, a utility group indirectly controlled by Suez which is Belgium's principal supplier of electricity.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, already angry with Paris over French carmaker Renault SA's decision to close its Vilvoorde plant, has voiced concern that a Lyonnaise-Suez pact might harm Belgian interests.
Le Monde, however, said it appeared that Dehaene had been offered assurances on Tractebel's autonomy following a merger.
One investment banker said Suez's financial strength was in any case more important to the success of an eventual merger than industrial synergies between Tractebel and Lyonnaise.
